sections.text: CPU busy most of the time, or active memory near all it has. More vCPUs or memory suggested (amber). Together: 4 vCPUs and 0 GB more.

rows: Memory taken back: up to 1024 MB ballooned; the ESXi host was short of memory (its other VMs, or the host itself): check the host before resizing.
sections.text: The ESXi host took memory back from these VMs (ballooning, swapping) or a limit caps them: they run slower than their size says. Not a sizing problem of the VM: its host, or the limit.

sections.text: More vCPUs or memory than they use: the suggested size (green) still leaves room - CPU sized to 70% busy, memory to its active memory plus 100%. Together they free 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory for other VMs.

sections.title: Not enough history

lines: From vCenter's own statistics of the last 30 days (2-hour averages) - the hypervisor's measurements, nothing from inside the guests - and each VM's busiest day of the last year (daily averages).

CPU: the busiest 5% of the time is left out (the 95th percentile), or the year's busiest day is used when it was busier; vCPUs are suggested so that use would be about 70%, never more than 50% fewer at once, at least 2 (Windows 2). 85% or more is too small.
CPU ready is the time a VM waited for a physical CPU: 5% or more is said. It often means too many vCPUs, or a busy host.

Memory (the less certain one): vCenter sees the memory a guest touched in the last minutes (active memory), not what it needs - file caches and databases want more. So the suggestion is its active memory plus 100%, never more than 50% less at once, at least 2 GB (Windows 4), and only when it is 25% and 2 GB smaller or more. Active memory at 90% or more is too small.
Suggestions only: nothing was changed. Check a VM's own peaks (month end, patching, backups) before resizing it; removing vCPUs or memory needs the VM shut down.
